translations.text: These are the names of the sons of Israel who went to Egypt with their father Jacob. Each one entered with his entire household.
Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah,
Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin,
Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher.
Joseph was already in Egypt. All the people descended from Jacob numbered seventy [?].
Joseph died, along with all his brothers and that entire generation.
The Israelites grew and multiplied, spread out, and became very strong. The land caused them to multiply.
Another king arose over Egypt, who did not know Joseph.
He said to his people, “Look, the nation of the Israelites is a great multitude, and they are stronger than we are.”
Come, let us devise a plan against them, so that they do not multiply and, if war breaks out against us, join our enemies, fight against us, and leave the land.”
He appointed overseers over them in their work, to oppress them with labor. They built fortified cities for Pharaoh: Pithom, Rameses, and On, which is the City of the Sun.
But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and became exceedingly strong. The Egyptians detested the Israelites.
They made their lives miserable with hard labor in mortar and brickmaking, with all the work in the fields, and with every task in which they ruthlessly made them serve as slaves.
The king of Egypt spoke to the Hebrew midwives. The name of one was Shiphrah, and the name of the second was Puah.
He said, “When you come to serve as midwives to the Hebrew women as they are about to give birth, if the child is a boy, kill him; but if it is a girl, keep her alive.”
But the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt had commanded them. They kept the boys alive.
The king of Egypt summoned the Hebrew midwives and said to them, “Why have you done this and kept the boys alive?”
The midwives said to Pharaoh, “The Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women when they give birth. They give birth before the midwives come to them, and they were giving birth.”
God treated the midwives well, and the people multiplied and became very strong.
Because the midwives feared God, houses were built for them.
Pharaoh commanded all his people, saying, “Throw every boy born to the Hebrews into the water, but keep every girl alive.”
There was a man from the tribe of Levi who took a wife from among the daughters of Levi, and she became his wife.
She conceived and gave birth to a son. They saw that he was beautiful and hid him for three months.
Because they could no longer hide him, his mother got a basket for him, coated it with pitch, put the little boy in it, and placed it among the reeds beside the river.
His sister stood watching from a distance to find out what would happen to him.
Pharaoh’s daughter came down to the river to bathe, and her servants were walking along the river. She saw the basket among the reeds, sent her servant, and had it brought to her.
She opened it and saw the little boy crying in the basket. Pharaoh’s daughter felt pity for him and said, “This is one of the Hebrews’ children.”
His sister said to Pharaoh’s daughter, “Would you like me to call a nursing woman from among the Hebrews to nurse the little boy for you?”
Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, “Go.” So the little girl went and called the child’s mother.
Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, “Look after this child and nurse him for me, and I will pay you your wages.” So the woman took the child and nursed him.
When the child grew older, she brought him to Pharaoh’s daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses, saying, “I drew him out of the water.”
During those many days, when Moses had grown up, he went out to his fellow Israelites. As he observed their suffering, he saw an Egyptian man beating a Hebrew, one of his fellow Israelites.
He looked this way and that, and when he saw no one, he killed the Egyptian and hid him in the sand.
The next day he went out and saw two Hebrew men fighting with each other. He said to the one who was doing wrong, “Why are you hitting your neighbor?”

But the man said to him, “Who appointed you ruler and judge over us? Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?” Moses became afraid and said, “So the matter has become known in this way!”
Pharaoh heard about this matter and sought to kill Moses. But Moses fled from Pharaoh’s presence and settled in the land of Midian. When he came to the land of Midian, he sat down by a well.
The priest of Midian had seven daughters who tended their father’s sheep. They came and drew water until they filled the trough, to water the sheep of their father Jethro.
But the shepherds came and drove them away. Moses got up and rescued them and their sheep from the shepherds. He drew water for them and watered their sheep.
When they came to their father Jethro, he said to them, “Why have you come back so quickly today?”
They said, “An Egyptian man rescued us from the shepherds. He drew water for us and watered our sheep.”
He said to his daughters, “Where is he? Why did you leave the man behind like that? Call him so that he may eat some bread.”
Moses stayed with the man, and the man gave Moses his daughter Zipporah as his wife.
She became pregnant and bore a son. Moses named him Gershom, saying, “I am a foreigner in a land that is not my own.”
After those many days, the king of Egypt died. The Israelites groaned because of their harsh labor and cried out. Their cry because of their labor went up to God.
God heard their cry and their groaning, and God remembered his covenant, which he had established with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
God looked upon the Israelites and remembered.
Moses was tending the sheep of his father-in-law, the priest of Midian. He led the sheep to the far side of the wilderness and came to the mountain of God, Horeb, the mountain of the Lord God.
The angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire from within a bush. He saw that the bush was ablaze with fire, but the bush was not being burned up.
Moses said, “I will go and look at this great sight, to see why the bush is not burning up.”
When the Lord saw that he was going to come closer, the Lord called to him from within the bush, saying, “Moses, Moses!” He replied, “What is it?”
He said to him, “Do not come close to this place. Take the sandals off your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.”
He also said to him, “I am the God of your father Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Moses turned his face away, for he was afraid to look upon God.
The Lord said to Moses, “I have indeed seen the oppression of my people who are in Egypt, and I have heard their cry because of the taskmasters, for I know their suffering.”

And I have come down to rescue them from the hands of the Egyptians, to bring them out of the land of Egypt and lead them into a good and spacious land, a land flowing with milk and honey, to the place of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, Girgashites, and Jebusites.
Now, look, the cry of the Israelites has come up to me, and I myself have seen the distress in which the Egyptians oppress them.
Now come, and I will send you to Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, so that you may bring my people, the Israelites, out of the land of Egypt.
Moses said to God, “Who am I to go to Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, and bring the people out of the land of Egypt?”
God said to Moses, “I will be with you, and this will be a sign to you that I am the one sending you: when you bring my people out of the land of Egypt, you will worship God on the mountain.”
Moses said before God, “Look, I will go to the Israelites and tell them, ‘The God of your ancestors has sent me to you.’ If they ask me, ‘What is his name?’ what shall I tell them?”
God said to Moses, “I am the one who exists. This is what you are to tell the Israelites: ‘The one who exists has sent me to you.’”

God also said to Moses, “This is what you are to tell the Israelites: ‘The Lord, the God of your ancestors, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is how I am to be remembered from generation to generation.”

Go and gather the elders of the Israelites, and tell them, ‘The Lord, the God of your ancestors, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, appeared to me and said, “I have indeed visited you and seen what has happened to you in the land of Egypt.”’

I said, “I will bring you out of the affliction inflicted by the Egyptians and up to the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Girgashites, and Jebusites, to a land flowing with milk and honey.”

They will listen to you. You and the elders of the Israelites are to go to Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, and tell him, ‘The Lord, the God of the Hebrews, has called us. So we will go a three-day journey into the wilderness, so that we may offer sacrifices before the Lord our God.’
But I know that Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, will not let you go except under the force of a strong hand.
I will stretch out my hand and strike the Egyptians with all my wonders that I will perform among them. After these things, he will let you go.
And I will give this people favor in the eyes of the Egyptians. When you leave, you will not go away empty-handed.

Each woman will receive silver objects, gold objects, and clothes from her neighbor and the woman who lives in her house. You will put them on your sons and daughters, and you will plunder the Egyptians.
Moses answered, saying, “What if they do not believe me [?] and do not listen to me? For they will say, ‘God has not appeared to you.’ What will I tell them?”
The Lord said to him, “What is that in your hand?” He said, “It is a staff.”
He said to him, “Throw it down on the ground.” It became a snake, and Moses ran away from it.
The Lord said to him, “Stretch out your hand and take hold of its tail.” He stretched out his hand and took hold of its tail, and it became a staff in his hand.
“So that they may believe you, that the Lord, the God of their ancestors, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you.”
The Lord also said to him, “Put your hand inside your clothing, against your chest.” He put his hand inside his clothing and brought it out again, and his hand had become like snow.
He said to him again, “Put your hand inside your clothing, against your chest.” He put his hand inside his clothing and brought it out again, and it had returned to the color of his flesh.
But if they are not convinced by you through the first sign, they will be convinced by you through the last sign.

If they are not convinced by you through these two signs and do not listen to your voice, take some water from the river and pour it onto the dry ground. The water you take from the river will become blood on the dry ground.

Moses said to the Lord, “I beg you, Lord, I am not a good speaker—not before yesterday or the day before, nor today, nor since you began speaking to your servant. For my tongue is slow and my voice is weak.”
The Lord said to Moses, “Who gave a human being a mouth? And who made the deaf and the mute, the person who can see and the blind person? Was it not I, the Lord God?
Now, then, go. I will open your mouth and teach you what to say.”
But Moses said, “I beg you, Lord, find someone else who is capable and send him.”

The Lord became furious with Moses and said, “There is Aaron your brother, the Levite. I know that he will certainly speak with you. Look, he is coming out to meet him. He will see you and rejoice in his heart.
You will speak to him and put my words into his mouth. I will open his mouth and your mouth and teach you both what to do.
He will speak with you before the people and serve as your mouth, while you will act for him before God.
Take in your hand this staff that turned into a snake; with it you will perform the signs.”
Moses went back to Jethro his father-in-law and said, “I will go back to my brothers who are in Egypt and see whether they are still alive.” Jethro said to Moses, “Go safely.”
After those many days, the king of Egypt died. The Lord said to Moses in the land of Midian, “Set out and go to Egypt, for everyone who was seeking your life has died.”
Moses took his wife and his children, put them on the beasts of burden, and returned to Egypt. Moses took in his hand the staff that came from God.
The Lord said to Moses, “As you go back to Egypt, be sure to perform before Pharaoh all the wonders I have put in your hands. But I will harden his heart so that he will not let the people go.”
You are to tell Pharaoh, ‘This is what the Lord says: Israel is my son, my firstborn.’
I told you, “Let my people go so that they may serve me.” If you refuse to let them go, look, I will kill your firstborn.’”
On the way, at the lodging place, an angel of the Lord met him and tried to kill him.
Zipporah took a stone and circumcised her son’s foreskin. She fell at his feet and said, “The blood from my son’s circumcision has stopped.”
He withdrew from her because she said, “The blood from my son’s circumcision has stopped.”
The Lord said to Aaron, “Go and meet Moses in the wilderness.” He went to meet him at the mountain of God, and they greeted one another.
Moses told his brother Aaron all the words the Lord had spoken and all the signs he had instructed him to perform.
Moses and Aaron went and gathered the elders of the Israelites.
Aaron told them all the words that God had instructed Moses to convey, and he performed the signs before the people.
The people believed and rejoiced because God had visited the Israelites and had seen their affliction. The people bowed down and worshiped the Lord.
After this, Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh and told him, “This is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: ‘Let my people go, so that they may celebrate a festival for me in the wilderness.’”
He said to them, “Who is this that I should obey him and let the Israelites go? I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go.”
They said to him, “The God of the Hebrews has called us. We will therefore go a three-day journey on foot so that we may offer sacrifices before our God, lest death or slaughter befall us.”
The king of Egypt said to them, “Moses and Aaron, why are you turning my people away from their work? Let each of you go about his work.”
Pharaoh said, “Look, the people of the land are now numerous. So let us not give them relief from their work.”
Pharaoh gave orders to the overseers of the people’s work and to the scribes, saying:
“You must no longer give the people straw for making bricks as you did before. Today let them go and gather straw for themselves.”

“You must impose on them the quota of bricks they usually make each day. You must not reduce it at all, for they are idle. That is why they cry out, saying, ‘Let us go and offer sacrifices before our God.’
“Let these men’s work become heavier, so that they pay attention to it and do not pay attention to empty words.”
The overseers and scribes became agitated, speaking before the people and saying, “This is what Pharaoh says: ‘From now on, I will not give you straw.’
“Go and gather straw for yourselves wherever you can find it, for nothing will be deducted from your quota of bricks.”
The people scattered throughout Egypt to gather stubble for themselves to use as straw.
The taskmasters kept pressuring them, saying, “Complete the work assigned to you each day, just as you did when you were given straw.”
The Israelite foremen whom Pharaoh’s taskmasters had appointed over them were beaten and asked, “Why have you not completed your quota of bricks today as you did yesterday and the day before?”
The Israelite foremen went in and cried out before Pharaoh, saying, “Why are you treating your servants this way?”
“No straw is given to your servants, yet they tell us, ‘Make the quota of bricks.’ Look, your servants have been beaten! Will you treat your people unjustly?”
He said to them, “You are idle! You are lazy people! That is why you say, ‘Let us go so that you can offer sacrifices before our God.’”
“Now go and work. No straw will be given to you, but you must deliver the quota of bricks.”
The Israelite foremen saw that they were in trouble when they were told, “You must not reduce the quota of bricks assigned to you each day.”
As they came away from Pharaoh, they met Moses and Aaron, who were coming to meet them.
They said to them, “May God look upon you and judge, because you have made our odor offensive before Pharaoh and before his servants, putting a sword into his hands to kill us.”
Moses returned to the Lord, saying, “Lord, why have you afflicted your people? And why have you sent me to your people?”
“For ever since I went to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has afflicted your people, and you have not rescued your people.”
The Lord said to Moses, “Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh. With a strong hand he will let them go, and with a raised hand he will drive them out of his land.”
God spoke to Moses, saying, “I am the Lord.”
“I appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, being their God, but I did not reveal my name to them.”
“I also established my covenant with them to give them the land of the Canaanites, the land where they lived as foreigners.”
But I have heard the groaning of the Israelites, whom the Egyptians are enslaving, and I have remembered your covenant.
So go and tell the Israelites, ‘I am the Lord. I will bring you out from the oppression of the Egyptians and rescue you from slavery. I will redeem you with an uplifted arm and a great judgment.’
“‘I will take you as my people, and I will be your God. You will know that I am the Lord your God, who brings you out from the oppression of the Egyptians.’
“‘I will bring you into the land that I stretched out my hand to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. I will give it to you as an inheritance. I am the Lord.’”
Moses spoke this way to the Israelites, but they did not listen to him because of their discouragement and their hard labor.
Then the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:
“Go in and speak to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, so that he will let the Israelites leave his land.”
But Moses spoke before the Lord, saying, “Look, the Israelites have not listened to me. How will Pharaoh listen, when I do not know how to speak?”
The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron and instructed them to go to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt.
These are the heads of their ancestral households. The sons of Reuben, Israel’s firstborn, were Hanoch and Pallu, Hezron and Carmi. This is the family of Reuben.
The sons of Simeon were Jemuel, Jamin, Lot, Achim, Zohar, and Saul, the son of the Phoenician woman. These are the families of the households of Simeon.
These are the names of the sons of Levi according to their clans: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Levi lived for 137 years.
These are the sons of Gershon: Libni and Shimei, the households of their families.
The sons of Kohath were Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. Kohath lived for 133 years.
The sons of Merari were Mahli and Mushi. These are the ancestral households of Levi according to their clans.
Amram took Jochebed, the daughter of his father's brother, as his wife. She bore him Aaron, Moses, and Miriam, their sister. Amram lived for 134 years.
The sons of Izhar were Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri.
The sons of Uzziel were Elizaphan and Sithri.
Aaron took Elisheba, the daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon, as his wife. She bore him Nadab, Abiud, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
The sons of Korah were Assir, Elkanah, and Abitham. These are the clans of Korah.
Eleazar, Aaron's son, took a wife from among the daughters of Putiel. She bore him Phinehas. These are the leaders and families of the Levites according to their clans.
These are Aaron and Moses, whom God told to bring the Israelites out of Egypt with their multitude.
These are the ones who spoke to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and brought the Israelites out of Egypt. These are Aaron and Moses.
On the day when the Lord spoke to Moses in Egypt,
the Lord spoke to Moses, saying, “I am the Lord. Tell Pharaoh, king of Egypt, the things I will tell you.”
Moses said before the Lord, “Look, I am a poor speaker. How will Pharaoh listen to me?”
The Lord said to Moses, “Look, I have made you a god to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother will be your prophet.
You must tell him everything I command you, and Aaron your brother will speak to Pharaoh so that he lets the Israelites leave the land of Egypt.
“But I will harden Pharaoh’s heart and multiply my signs and wonders in the land of Egypt.”
Pharaoh will not listen to you, but I will bring my hand down upon Egypt and, by my power, bring my people Israel out of the land of Egypt with great punishment.
Then all the Egyptians will know that I am the Lord, when I stretch out my hand over Egypt to bring the Israelites out from among them.
Moses and Aaron did these things just as the Lord had commanded them.
Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron his brother was eighty-three, when he was about to speak to Pharaoh.
The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying:

“If Pharaoh speaks to you and says, ‘Give us a sign or a wonder,’ you must say to your brother Aaron, ‘Take the staff and throw it down on the ground before Pharaoh and his servants, and it will become a snake.’”
Moses and Aaron went in before Pharaoh and his servants and did these things just as the Lord had told them. Aaron threw down the staff before Pharaoh and his servants, and it became a snake.
Pharaoh summoned the wise men of Egypt and the sorcerers. The magicians of Egypt also did these things through their spells.
Each of them threw his staff down on the ground, and they became snakes. But Aaron’s staff swallowed their staffs.
Pharaoh's heart grew stubborn, and he did not listen to them, just as the Lord had told them.
Then the Lord said to Moses, “Pharaoh's heart has become hard, so that he will not let the people go.
Go to Pharaoh in the morning. Look, he is going out to the water. Stand on the riverbank to meet him, and take in your hands the staff that turned into a snake.
Say to him, ‘The Lord, the God of the Hebrews, sent me to you, saying, “Let my people go so that they may worship me in the wilderness.” But look, you have not listened up to now.
This is what the Lord says: “By this you will know that I am the Lord. Look, I will strike the river and its waters with my staff that is in my hand, and it will turn into blood.
The fish in the river will die, and the Egyptians will not be able to drink water from the river and its waters.”’”

Then the Lord said to Moses, “Tell Aaron your brother, ‘Take the staff and stretch it out in your hand over the waters of Egypt, over their rivers, their canals, their marshes, and all the water they have, so that they become blood. There will be blood throughout the whole land of Egypt, even in wooden and stone containers.’”

Moses and Aaron did these things just as the Lord had commanded them. Aaron raised the staff and struck the water in the river before Pharaoh and his servants, and all the water in the river turned into blood.
The fish in the river died, and the river water stank. The Egyptians could not drink water from the river, and there was blood throughout the whole land of Egypt.
The Egyptian magicians also did these things through their sorcery. Pharaoh's heart grew hard, and he did not listen to them, just as the Lord had told them.
Pharaoh turned and went into his house, and he paid no attention to this either.
All the Egyptians dug around the river to get water to drink, because they could not drink water from the river.
Seven days passed after the Lord struck the river.
Then the Lord said to Moses, “Go in to Pharaoh and tell him, ‘This is what the Lord says: Let my people go so that they may worship me.
But if you are unwilling to let them go, look, I will strike all your territory with frogs.

The river will bring forth frogs. They will come up and enter your houses, your chambers, and your bedrooms, and climb onto your couches. They will enter the houses of your servants and your people, and your ovens and kneading troughs.
The frogs will come up onto you and your people.’”
The Lord said to Moses, “Tell Aaron your brother, ‘Stretch out the staff in your hand over the rivers, the canals, and the marshes, and bring up the frogs.’”
Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs covered the whole land of Egypt.
The magicians of Egypt also did these things through their spells, and they brought frogs up onto the land of Egypt.

Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said to them, “Pray to the Lord for me, so that he will remove these frogs from me and my people. Then I will let the people go so that they may offer sacrifices to the Lord their God.”

Moses said to Pharaoh, “Set the time with me: when should I pray for you, your servants, and your people, so that these frogs are removed from you, your servants, your people, and your houses? They will remain only in the river.”
But he said, “Tomorrow I will do as you have said, so that you may know that there is no one besides the Lord.
The frogs will be removed from you, from your houses and your courtyards, from your servants and your people. They will remain only in the river.”
Moses and Aaron left Pharaoh, and Moses cried out to the Lord about the appointed time for the frogs, as Pharaoh had specified.
The Lord did as Moses had said. The frogs died in the houses, the courtyards, and the fields.
They gathered the frogs into heaps upon heaps, and the land stank.
But when Pharaoh saw that there was relief, he hardened his heart and did not listen to them, just as the Lord had told them.
The Lord said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Stretch out your hand with the staff and strike the dust of the ground, so that gnats may appear on people and animals throughout the whole land of Egypt.’”
Aaron stretched out the staff in his hand and struck the dust of the ground. Gnats appeared on people and animals, and all the dust of the ground became gnats throughout the whole land of Egypt.
The magicians also tried to do this with their spells, to bring forth gnats, but they could not. The gnats were on people and animals.
Then the magicians said to Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God.” But Pharaoh’s heart grew hard, and he did not listen to them, just as the Lord had told them.

The Lord said to Moses, “Get up early in the morning and stand before Pharaoh. Look, he is coming out to the water. Say to him, ‘This is what the Lord says: Let my people go so that they may serve me.

But if you are unwilling to let my people go, look, I will send dogflies upon you, your servants, your people, and your houses. The Egyptians’ houses will be filled with dogflies, as will the ground where they live.
On that day I will honor the land of Goshen, where my people live: there will be no dogflies there, so that you may know that I am the Lord, the Lord of the whole earth.
I will make a distinction between my people and your people. Tomorrow this sign will take place upon the land.’”
The Lord did this. Great numbers of dogflies came upon Pharaoh’s houses, into his servants’ houses, and throughout the whole land. The whole land was ruined by the dogflies.
Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said to them, “Go and offer sacrifices to your God here in the land.”

But Moses said, “It cannot be done this way, because what we will sacrifice to the Lord our God is abhorrent to the Egyptians. If we sacrifice what is abhorrent to the Egyptians before their eyes, they will stone us.
We will travel a three-day journey into the wilderness and offer sacrifices to the Lord our God, just as he has told us.”
Pharaoh said, “I will let you go to offer sacrifices to the Lord your God in the wilderness, but you must not go far away. So pray to the Lord for me.”

Moses said to him, “Look, I will leave you and pray to God for you, so that tomorrow the dogflies will stop and withdraw from you, your servants, and your people. But do not continue to deceive us, Pharaoh, by refusing to let my people go to offer sacrifices to the Lord our God in the wilderness.”
Moses left Pharaoh and prayed to the Lord God.
The Lord did as Moses had said. He removed the dogflies from Pharaoh, his servants, and his people. Not a single one remained.
Pharaoh hardened his heart this time too and was unwilling to let the people go.
The Lord said to Moses, “Go in to Pharaoh and tell him, ‘This is what the Lord, the God of the Hebrews, says: Let my people go so that they may serve me.’
“If you are unwilling to let my people go but still hold on to them,
“Look, the Lord’s hand will strike your livestock in the fields—the horses, the beasts of burden, the camels, the cattle, and the sheep—with a very great loss of life.”
I will show my glory among the livestock of the Egyptians and among the livestock of the Israelites, so that nothing belonging to any of the Israelites dies.
God set a time, saying, “Tomorrow the Lord will do this in the land.”
The Lord did this the next day. All the Egyptians’ livestock died, but none of the Israelites’ livestock died.
Pharaoh saw that nothing belonging to any of the Israelites had died. But Pharaoh’s heart became hard, and he did not let the people go.
The Lord said to Moses and Aaron, “Take handfuls of soot from a furnace, and let Moses throw it up toward the sky in front of Pharaoh and his servants.
It will become dust over the whole land, and festering boils will break out on people and livestock throughout the land of Egypt.”
Moses took the soot from the furnace and threw it up toward the sky in front of Pharaoh. Festering boils broke out on people and livestock.
The magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils, for the boils had broken out on the magicians and throughout the land of Egypt.
But the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not listen to them, just as the Lord had told Moses.

The Lord said to Moses, “Get up early in the morning, stand before Pharaoh, and tell him, ‘This is what the Lord, the God of the Hebrews, says: Let my people go so that they may serve me in the wilderness.
For this time I will send all my plagues upon your heart and upon the hearts of your servants and your people, so that you may see that there is no one like me in all the earth.
For now I will stretch out my hand and strike you, and I will kill your people, and you will be wiped off the earth.
For this reason you have been kept alive: so that I may show my power through you and my name may be proclaimed throughout the earth.
You are still holding on to my people, refusing to let them go.
“Look, at this time tomorrow I will rain down extremely heavy hail upon you, such as has never occurred in Egypt from the day it was founded until today.”

Now hurry and bring in your livestock and everything you have in the fields. For all the people and livestock found in the fields who have not gone into the houses will die when the hail falls on them.’”
Those among Pharaoh’s servants who feared the Lord’s word brought their livestock into their houses.
But those who paid no attention in their hearts to the Lord’s word left their livestock in the fields.
The Lord said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward the sky, and hail will fall over the whole land of Egypt, on the people, the livestock, and every plant on the ground.”
Moses stretched out his hand toward the sky, and the Lord sent thunder and hail. He poured it down over the whole land of Egypt.
The hail was very heavy, with fire flashing within it. Nothing like it had happened in Egypt since it became a nation.
The hail struck throughout the land of Egypt, striking people and livestock alike. The hail also struck down every plant in the fields.
Except in the land of Goshen, where the Israelites were, no hail fell there.
Pharaoh sent for Moses and Aaron and said to them, “This time I have sinned. The Lord is righteous, but my people and I are wicked.”
“Pray for me before the Lord so that God’s thunder may stop and occur no more, and so that the hail and fire may stop. I will let you go, and you will no longer have to stay.”

Moses said to him, “Look, I will go outside the city and spread out my hands before the Lord. The thunder accompanying the hail will stop, and there will be no more rain, so that you may know that the earth belongs to the Lord.”
“But as for you and your servants, I know that you do not yet fear the Lord.”
The flax and barley were destroyed, for the barley had matured and the flax had produced seed.
But the wheat and the spelt were not struck down, because they were late crops.
Moses left Pharaoh and went outside the city. He spread out his [?] hands toward the Lord, and the thunder and hail stopped. The rain no longer poured down on the ground.
When Pharaoh saw that the rain, hail, and thunder had stopped, he continued to sin. He hardened his heart and the hearts of his servants.
Pharaoh hardened his heart and did not let the Israelites go, just as the Lord had told Moses.
The Lord said to Moses, “Go to Pharaoh, for I am the one who made his heart and the hearts of his servants stubborn, so that afterward my signs may come upon them,
so that you may tell your children, and your children may tell their children, what I did to the Egyptians and all the signs I performed among them, and so that you may know that I am the Lord.”

Moses and Aaron went in before Pharaoh and said to him, “This is what the Lord, the God of the Hebrews, says: ‘How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me? Let my people go so that they may worship me.
But if you refuse to let my people go, look: at this time tomorrow I will bring an enormous swarm of locusts over all your territory.

It will cover the surface of the land, so that you will not be able to see the ground. It will eat everything on the surface of the land, including what the hail left you, and it will eat every tree growing on the land.

Your houses, your servants’ houses, and all the houses throughout the land of Egypt will be filled with them. Your fathers and your fathers’ fathers have never seen anything like this, from the day they came to be on the earth until today.’” Then Moses turned and left Pharaoh.
Pharaoh’s servants said to him, “How long will this man be a trap for us? Let the men go so that they may worship the Lord their God. Or do you want to learn that Egypt has been utterly destroyed?”
Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh. He said to them, “Go and worship your God. But who exactly will be going?”
Moses said to him, “We will go with our young and our old. We will go with our sons and daughters, our sheep and our cattle, because it is a festival of the Lord our God.”
He said to them, “May it be so: may the Lord be with you! Do you really think I will let you go, along with your households? Look, evil lies before you.
If that is how it is, let the men go instead, and worship your God, for that is what you are asking for.” Then they were driven out of Pharaoh’s presence.

The Lord said to Moses and Aaron, “Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt, so that the locusts may come upon the land and eat every plant on the land and all the fruit of the trees that the hail left.”

Moses stretched out his staff toward the sky, and the Lord, by his power, brought a south wind over the land throughout that whole day and the whole night. When morning came, the south wind brought the locusts.

It carried them over the whole land of Egypt, and they settled throughout all the territory of Egypt in enormous numbers. There had never been locusts like these before, and afterward there were never any like them.

They covered the entire surface of the land, and the land was ruined. They ate every plant in the land and all the fruit of the trees that the hail had left. Nothing green remained on the trees or among any of the plants in the fields throughout the whole land of Egypt.
Pharaoh hurried to summon Moses and Aaron, saying, “I have sinned before the Lord your God and against you.
Now forgive my sin this once more, and pray to the Lord your God, so that he may take this death away from me.”
Moses left Pharaoh and prayed to God.
The Lord turned a strong wind from the sea, took the locusts, and threw them into the Red Sea. Not a single locust remained anywhere in the whole land of Egypt.
Pharaoh hardened his heart and did not let the Israelites go.
Then the Lord said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward heaven, and let darkness come over the land of Egypt—a darkness that can be felt.”
Moses stretched out his hand toward the sky, and darkness and a storm came over the whole land of Egypt for three days.
No one saw anyone else for three days, nor did anyone rise from where they were sitting for three days. But all the Israelites had light in everything they did.
Then Pharaoh called Moses and said, “Go and worship the Lord your God, but leave the sheep and cattle. Take your household with you.”
Moses said to him, “It will not be so. Rather, you yourself will also give us burnt offerings and sacrifices to offer up to the Lord our God.

All our livestock will go with us, and we will not leave a hoof behind. For we will take some of them to worship the Lord our God. We do not know what we will offer up to the Lord our God until we arrive at that place.”
But the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not want to release them.
Pharaoh said, “Get away from me! Be careful not to see my face again from now on, for on the day you appear before me, you will die.”
Moses said, “You have said it. I will not appear before your face again.”

Then the Lord said to Moses, “There is still one more plague that I will bring upon Pharaoh and upon Egypt. After that, he will release you from this place. When he releases you, he will drive you all out at once, forcibly.
So speak secretly in the people’s ears, and let each man ask his neighbor, and each woman her neighbor, for silver objects, gold objects, and clothing.”
The Lord gave his people favor in the eyes of the Egyptians, and they gave to them. Moreover, the man Moses became great in the eyes of the Egyptians and in the eyes of Pharaoh and his servants.
And Moses said, “This is what the Lord says: ‘At midnight I am coming into Egypt,

and every firstborn in the land of Egypt will die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sits on his throne, down to the firstborn of the servant woman who is at the grinding place, and the firstborn of every animal.
There will be a great cry throughout the whole land of Egypt, such as has never occurred and will never occur afterward.
But among all the Israelites, not a dog will make a sound with its [?], against either a person or an animal, so that you may see the wonders the Lord will perform in the midst of Egypt and Israel.
All your servants will come down to our feet and bow to me, saying, ‘Leave, with all your people whom you lead.’ After that, I will leave.” Then Moses went out from Pharaoh in anger.
Then the Lord said to Moses, “Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that I may multiply my signs and wonders in the land of Egypt before Pharaoh.”
Moses and Aaron performed the signs before Pharaoh, but the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he was unwilling to let the Israelites leave the land of Egypt.
Then the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying,
“This month is to be the beginning of the months for you. It is to be the first of the months of the year for you.
Speak to the whole congregation of the Israelites, saying, ‘On the tenth day of this month, each person must take a sheep for their ancestral household, one sheep for each house.’
But if there are too few in the household to be sufficient for the sheep, let him share it with his nearest neighbor according to the number of people. Count each person’s share toward one sheep.
You must take a perfect male lamb, one year old, with no blemish on it. You must take it from your lambs or your young goats.
You must keep it until the fourteenth day of this month. Then the entire assembly of the congregation of the Israelites must slaughter it in the evening.
You must take some of its blood and sprinkle it on the two doorposts and on the houses in which they will eat it.
They must eat its meat that night, roasted over a fire. You must eat unleavened bread with bitter herbs.
You must not eat any of it raw or boiled in water, but roasted over a fire, with its head, its feet, and its internal organs.
You must not leave any of it until morning, and you must not break a bone in it. Whatever remains of it until morning you must burn in a fire.
You must eat it this way: with your belts fastened, your sandals on your feet, and your staffs in your hands. You must eat it in haste, because it is the Lord’s Passover.
I will go out through Egypt that night and kill every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from humans to livestock. I will carry out punishment against all the gods of the Egyptians. I am the Lord.
The blood will be a sign for you on the houses where you are. I will see the blood and protect you, and no plague will destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt.
This day must be a memorial for you. You must celebrate it as a festival to the Lord for the [?] after you. You must celebrate it as a festival to the Lord, as a permanent ordinance forever.

For seven days you must eat unleavened bread. From the very first day you must remove leaven from your houses. Whoever eats anything leavened, from the first day through the seventh day, will be cut off from Israel.
The first day must be called holy, and the seventh day must be called holy for you. You must not do any work of service on it, except what each person needs; that alone you may do.
You must keep these commandments, for on this day I will bring your multitudes out of the land of Egypt. You must observe this day throughout your generations as a permanent ordinance forever.
From the evening of the fourteenth day of the first month, you must eat unleavened bread until the evening of the twenty-first day of the month.
For seven days no yeast is to be found in your houses. Whoever eats anything leavened is to be cut off from the congregation of Israel, whether a foreigner or a native of the land.
You must not eat anything leavened. In all your homes you must eat unleavened bread.
Moses called all the elders of the Israelites and said to them, “Go and get sheep for yourselves according to your families, and slaughter the Passover sacrifice.”

You must take a bunch of hyssop and dip it in the blood at the doorway. Sprinkle the lintel and the two doorposts with the blood at the doorway. None of you must go outside the door of your house until morning.

The Lord will come to strike the Egyptians. He will see the blood on the lintel and on the two doorposts, and the Lord will come over the doorway and will not let the destroyer enter your houses to strike you.
You must keep this instruction as an ordinance for you and your children forever.
When you enter the land that the Lord will give you, as he said, you must observe this rite.
And when your children say to you, “What is this ceremony?”

You are to tell them, “This Passover that we celebrate is a sacrifice to the Lord, because he protected the houses of the Israelites when he struck the houses of the Egyptians, but saved ours.” Then the people bowed down and worshiped the Lord.
The Israelites went and did as the Lord had commanded Moses and Aaron. That is what they did.

At midnight, the Lord struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat on his throne, to the firstborn of the female captive in the dungeon, and every firstborn of the livestock.
Pharaoh rose during the night, along with his servants and all the Egyptians. A great cry arose throughout the whole land of Egypt, for there was no house in which someone had not died.
Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron during the night and said to them, “Get up and leave my people, both you and the Israelites. Go and serve your God, as you have said.”
Take your sheep and your cattle and go. And bless me too.”
The Egyptians pressed the people to drive them out of the land quickly, for they said, “We are all going to die.”
The people took their dough, wrapped in their clothes, on their shoulders.
The Israelites did as the Lord had commanded Moses. They asked the Egyptians for silver objects, gold objects, and clothing.
The Lord gave his people favor in the Egyptians’ eyes, and they gave them what they asked for. Thus they plundered the Egyptians.
The Israelites set out from Rameses for Succoth. There were six hundred thousand on foot, apart from their dependents.
A mixed multitude also went up with them, along with their sheep, their cattle, and their many livestock.

They baked the dough they had brought out of Egypt into unleavened cakes, for it had not yet risen. The Egyptians had driven them out, and they could not stay or even prepare bread for themselves for the journey.
The Israelites lived in the land of Egypt and the land of Canaan, they and their ancestors, for four hundred and thirty years.
After four hundred and thirty years, all the Lord’s army came out of Egypt.

That night is the first vigil for the Lord, when he brought them out of the land of Egypt. That night is the first vigil for the Lord, to be observed by all the Israelites throughout their generations.
The Lord said to Moses, “This is the law of the Passover: no foreigner may eat any of it.
Every slave bought with money must be circumcised by you; afterward they may eat some of it.
No foreign resident or hired worker may eat any of it.
They must eat it in one house. You must not take any of its meat outside the house, and you must not break any of its bones.
The whole congregation of the Israelites is to do this.

If a foreigner comes to live among you to celebrate the Passover, you must circumcise every male belonging to him. Afterward he may come forward to celebrate it, and he will be like a native of that land. No uncircumcised person may eat any of it.
There will be one law for the native and for the foreigner who comes to live among you.”
The Israelites did as the Lord had commanded Moses and Aaron.
On that very day, the Lord brought the Israelites out of the land of Egypt with their entire company.
The Lord said to Moses:
“Consecrate to me every firstborn that is born, every male that comes forth among the Israelites, whether human or animal. It will belong to me.”

Moses said to the people, “Remember this day on which you came out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of your slavery, for with a mighty hand he brought you out of this place. You must not eat anything leavened.
For today you are coming out, in the new month.

When the Lord your God brings you into the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Hivites, Amorites, Girgashites, Perizzites, and Jebusites—the land the Lord swore to your fathers to give you, a land flowing with milk and honey—you must observe this act of worship in this month.
For six days you must eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there is a festival to the Lord.
You must eat unleavened bread for seven days. Nothing that contains leaven, nor any leaven, may be seen anywhere within your borders.
On that day you must tell your son, ‘This is because of what the Lord God did for me when I came out of Egypt.’
It shall be a sign on your hand and a reminder before your eyes, so that the law of the Lord may be in your mouth, for with a strong hand the Lord your God brought you out of Egypt.
You shall observe this law at the appointed times of its hours, from its days to its hours.
When the Lord your God brings you into the land of the Canaanites, as he swore to your ancestors, and gives it to you,

you shall set apart for the Lord your God every male that opens the womb. Every male that opens the womb among your cattle and your livestock, those that belong to you, you shall consecrate to the Lord.
Every donkey that opens the womb you shall exchange for a sheep. But if you do not exchange it, you shall redeem it. Every human firstborn among your sons you shall redeem.
If your son asks you afterward, you shall tell him, “With a strong hand the Lord brought us out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of our slavery.”

“And when Pharaoh’s heart stubbornly refused to let us go, he killed every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of humans to the firstborn of livestock. That is why I sacrifice before the Lord every male that opens the womb, and I will redeem every firstborn among my sons.”
It shall be a sign on your hand and something fixed before your eyes, for with a strong hand the Lord brought you out of the land of Egypt.

When Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them along the road of the Philistines, although it was nearby. For God said, “The people might change their minds when they see war and return to Egypt.”
God led the people around by the wilderness road toward the Red Sea. In the fifth generation, the Israelites came up out of Egypt.
Moses took Joseph’s bones with him, because Joseph had solemnly made the Israelites swear an oath, saying, “The Lord will surely come to your aid, and you must take my bones up with you.”
The Israelites set out from Succoth and traveled up to Etham, beside the wilderness.
God went ahead of them, by day in a pillar of cloud to lead them along the road, and by night in a pillar of fire.
The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night did not depart from before all the people.
The Lord spoke to Moses, saying,
“Speak to the Israelites: let them turn back and travel to a position opposite the farmstead, between Migdol and the sea, opposite Baal-zephon. Go ahead of them to the sea.”
“Pharaoh will say to his people, ‘The Israelites are lost, for the wilderness has closed them in.’”
But I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, and he will pursue them. I will gain glory through Pharaoh and his entire army, and all the Egyptians will know that I am the Lord.”

The king of Egypt was told that the people had fled. Pharaoh and his servants changed their minds about the people and said, “What have we done, letting the Israelites go so that they no longer serve us as slaves?”
Pharaoh harnessed all his chariots and gathered all his people together with him.
He took six hundred chosen chariots, along with all the Egyptians’ horses, and officers over them all.
The Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and the hearts of his servants, and they pursued the Israelites. The Israelites were traveling under a mighty hand.

The Egyptians pursued them and found them when they had reached the sea. Pharaoh and his servants drew near to the people, together with all the horses, his horsemen, and his entire army, opposite Terso and Baal-zephon.
The Israelites looked up and saw with their own eyes that the Egyptians were pursuing them. They were very afraid, and the Israelites cried out to the Lord.
They said to Moses, “Was it because there were no graves in Egypt that you brought us out to kill us in the wilderness? What have you done to us by bringing us out of Egypt?”
Is this not what we told you in Egypt, saying, 'Leave us alone so that we can serve the Egyptians'? For it is better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness.

Moses said to the people, 'Take courage, stand firm, and see the deliverance that comes from the Lord, which he will accomplish for you today. For the Egyptians you have seen today you will never see again, forever.'
The Lord is the one who fights for you; you must remain silent.
The Lord said to Moses, “Why are you crying out to me? Speak to the Israelites and tell them to go back.”
“Raise your staff and stretch out your hand over the sea until you divide it, so that the Israelites may enter the middle of the sea on dry ground.”
Look, I will harden the heart of Pharaoh and of all the Egyptians, so that they go in after them. I will gain glory through Pharaoh and his entire army, and through his chariots and his horses.
Then all the Egyptians will know that I am the Lord, when I gain glory through Pharaoh, his army, his chariots, and his horses.
The angel of the Lord, who was traveling ahead of the Israelites’ camp, moved and went behind them. The pillar of cloud that was in front of them also moved.
He went between the Egyptian camp and the camp of Israel. There was darkness and gloom, and they did not come near one another all that night.
Moses stretched out his hand over the sea. The Lord brought a strong south wind throughout the night and made the sea dry, and the water divided.
The Israelites went into the middle of the sea on dry ground, and the water was a wall for them on the right and on the left.
The Egyptians chased after the Israelites, and all Pharaoh’s horses, his chariots, and those riding them followed them into the middle of the sea.
During the morning watch, the Lord looked down upon the camp of the Egyptians with the pillar of fire and the cloud, and threw the camp of the Egyptians into confusion.
He bound the axles of their chariots and made them move with difficulty. The Egyptians said, “Let us flee from Israel, for the Lord is fighting for them against the Egyptians.”
The Lord said to Moses, 'Stretch out your hand over the sea so that the water may return to its place and cover the Egyptians, the chariots, and those riding on them.'
Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the water returned to its place as day approached. The Egyptians fled behind the water, and the Lord shook the Egyptians into the middle of the sea.
The water returned and covered the chariots, those riding on them, and Pharaoh's entire army, who were pursuing them into the sea. Not one of them remained.
But the Israelites walked on dry ground in the middle of the sea, and the water became a wall for them on their right and on their left.
The Lord saved Israel that day from the power of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead along the seashore.
And he saw the mighty power that the Lord had exercised against the Egyptians. The people feared the Lord and believed in God and in Moses his servant.
Then Moses and the Israelites sang this song to God. They said, “Say it: Let us praise God, for he has won glorious honor. He has thrown horse and rider into the sea.”
My helper and my protector has become my salvation. This is my God; I will give him glory. He is the God of my father; I will exalt him.
The Lord crushes wars; the Lord is his name.
Pharaoh's chariots and his army he threw into the sea. The chosen riders and the officers sank in the Red Sea.
The water covered them; they sank down into the depths like a stone.
Your right hand, Lord, has gained glory in power. Your right hand, Lord, has crushed the enemies.
And in the greatness of your glory you crushed those who opposed you. You sent out your wrath, and it consumed them like straw.
By the breath of your anger the water stood still. The waters became solid like a wall; the waters became solid in the middle of the sea.
The enemy said, “I will pursue them and catch them. I will divide the plunder and satisfy my soul. I will kill with my sword, and my hand will rule.”
You sent out your breath, and the sea covered them. They sank like lead in the mighty waters.
Who is like you among the gods, Lord? And who is like you, glorified among your holy ones? You are a wonder in your glories, performing signs.
You stretched out your right hand, and the earth swallowed them.
In righteousness you led your people whom you had saved. With your strength you encouraged them toward your holy dwelling place.
The nations heard and trembled; pains seized those who live in Philistia.
Then the leaders of Edom were troubled, and trembling seized the rulers of the Moabites. All the inhabitants of Canaan melted away.
Fear and trembling fell upon them. By the greatness of your arm, let them be silent until your people pass by them, Lord—the people you chose.
You will bring them into the mountain of your inheritance and plant them in your prepared dwelling place, which you prepared, Lord—the holy place that your hands prepared.
The Lord reigns from eternity to eternity and beyond.

For Pharaoh’s horses, his servants, all his chariots, and those riding them went into the sea, and the Lord brought the water of the Red Sea down over them. But the Israelites walked on dry ground in the middle of the sea.
Then Miriam the prophetess, Aaron’s sister, took her tambourine in her hands. All the women went out and followed her with their tambourines and dances.
Miriam walked ahead of them, saying, “Let us sing to the Lord with glory, for he has been glorified. A horse and its rider were thrown into the sea.”
Moses led the Israelites away from the Red Sea and brought them into the wilderness of Shur. They traveled for three days in the desert and found no water to drink.
They came to Marah, but they could not [?] water from Marah, because it was bitter. That is why they called that place “Bitterness.”
The people of Israel grumbled against Moses, saying, “What are we going to drink?”
Moses cried out to the Lord, and the Lord showed him a tree. He threw it into the water, and the water became sweet. There he established ordinances and laws for him, and there he tested him.

He said, “If you listen carefully to the voice of the Lord your God, do what pleases him in his sight, and keep all his commandments and ordinances, I will not bring upon you any of the diseases that I brought upon the Egyptians. For I am the Lord who heals you.”
Then they came to Elim. There were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees there, and they camped there beside the water.

They set out from Elim, and the whole assembly of the Israelites came to the wilderness of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after they came out of the land of Egypt.
The whole assembly of the Israelites grumbled against Moses and Aaron.

The Israelites said to them, “It would have been better if we had died in the land of Egypt, struck down by the Lord’s hand, when we sat by the pots of meat and ate bread until we were full. For you have brought us out into this desert to kill us and this whole assembly with hunger.”
“For in the evening you will know that it was the Lord who brought you out of the land of Egypt.”
“And in the morning you will see the glory of the Lord, because he has heard your grumbling against God. But who are we, that you grumble against us?”

Moses also said, “When the Lord gives you meat to eat in the evening and bread in the morning until you are full—for the Lord has heard the grumbling that you direct against us—who, then, are we? Your grumbling is not against us, but against God.”
Moses said to Aaron, “Tell the whole assembly of the Israelites, ‘Come into the Lord’s presence, for he has heard your grumbling.’”
Aaron spoke to the whole assembly of the Israelites. They turned toward the wilderness, and the glory of the Lord appeared in a cloud.
The Lord spoke to Moses, saying:

“I have heard the grumbling of the Israelites. Speak to them and say, ‘In the evening you will eat meat, and in the morning you will have your fill of bread. Then you will know that I am the Lord your God.’”
When evening came, a flock of quail came down and covered the camp. When morning came, dew was falling around the camp.
And look! There was something scattered over the surface of the wilderness, like coriander seed, white like frost on the ground.
When the Israelites saw it, they said to one another, “What is this?” For they did not know what it was. Moses said to them, “This is the bread that the Lord has given you to eat.”

“This is what the Lord has commanded you: Gather from it the amount allotted to each person, one measure per head, according to the number of your people. Each person is to gather for those who live with him.”
The Israelites did so and gathered it, some more and some less.
When they measured it with the measure, the one who had gathered more had no excess, and the one who had gathered less had no shortage. Each had gathered the amount allotted to him.
Moses said to them, “Do not let anyone leave any of it until morning.”
But they did not listen to Moses. Some left part of it until morning, and it bred worms and stank. Moses was angry with them.
They gathered it in the morning, each person the amount allotted to him. When the sun grew hot, it melted.
On the sixth day, they gathered double all the amounts allotted to them, two measures for each person. All the leaders of the assembly came in and told Moses.

Moses said to them, “This is what the Lord has said: Tomorrow is the Sabbath, a holy rest for the Lord. Bake what you intend to bake, and boil what you intend to boil. Set aside everything you have left over until morning.”
They left it until morning, as Moses had commanded them. It did not stink, nor did worms develop in it.
Moses said to them, “Eat it today, for today is the Lord’s Sabbath. You will not find any in the field.”
“For six days you will gather it for yourselves, but on the seventh day you will not find any, because it is the Sabbath, and none was created on that day.”
On the seventh day, some of the people went out to gather it for themselves, but they did not find any.
The Lord said to Moses, “How long will you refuse to obey my commandments and my law?”

“You have seen it: the Lord has given you this Sabbath day. That is why he gave you bread for two days on the sixth day. Each of you must stay in his house. Do not let any of you leave his place on the seventh day.”
And the people observed the Sabbath on the seventh day.
The Israelites called it manna. It was like coriander seed, white, and its taste was like a wafer made with honey.

Moses said, “This is what the Lord has commanded you: Fill the measure with manna and preserve it for your generations, so that they may see the bread you ate in the wilderness when the Lord brought you out of the land of Egypt.”
Moses said to his brother Aaron, “Take a golden jar and put a full measure of manna into it. Place it before God to preserve it for your generations.”
As the Lord had commanded Moses, Aaron placed it before the testimony to preserve it.
The Israelites ate manna for forty years, until they came to an inhabited land. They ate manna until they came to the border of Phoenicia.
The measure was one tenth of three measures.
Then the whole assembly of the Israelites set out from the wilderness of Sin, moving camp by camp at the Lord’s command. They came to Rephidim, but the people found no water to drink.
The people cursed Moses, saying, “Give us water so that we can drink.” Moses said to them, “Why are you cursing me? And why are you testing the Lord your God?”
The people thirsted for water there, and the people grumbled against Moses there, saying, “Why have you brought us out of Egypt to kill us, our children, and our livestock with thirst?”
Moses cried out to the Lord, saying, “What am I to do with these people? A little longer and they will stone me!”
The Lord said to Moses, “Go ahead of these people and take some of the elders of the people with you. Take in your hand the staff with which you struck the river, and go.
“Look, I am standing before you there on the rock at Horeb. Strike the rock, and water will flow out of it for the people to drink.” Moses did this in the sight of the Israelites, and they all drank.
He named that place “Testing” and “Cursing,” because they tested the Lord, saying, “Is the Lord among us or not?”
Then Amalek came and fought against Israel at Rephidim.
Moses said to Joshua, “Choose strong men for yourself, and go out and engage Amalek in battle tomorrow. Look, I will stand on top of the high ground with the staff of God in my hand.”
Joshua did as Moses had told him. He went out and engaged Amalek in battle. Moses, Aaron, and Hur stood on top of the hill.
Whenever Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed, but whenever Moses lowered his hands, Amalek prevailed.

Moses’ hands grew heavy, so they took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it. Aaron and Hur supported his hands, one on one side and the other on the other side. Moses’ hands remained steady until sunset.
Joshua cut down Amalek and all his people with the edge of the sword.
The Lord said to Moses, “Write this in a book as a memorial, and tell Joshua in his hearing that I will completely wipe out the memory of Amalek from under heaven.”
Moses built an altar to the Lord and named it “The Lord is my refuge.”
For with a hidden hand the Lord fights against Amalek from generation to generation.
Jethro, the priest of Midian and Moses’ father-in-law, heard about everything the Lord had done for his people Israel, for the Lord [?] Israel out of Egypt.
Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, took Zipporah, Moses’ wife, after Moses had sent her away,
along with his two sons. The name of one was Gershom, for he said, “I am a foreigner in a land that is not mine.”
The name of the second was Eliezer, for he said, “The God of my father is my helper, and he rescued me from Pharaoh’s hand.”
Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, brought Moses’ sons and wife to Moses in the wilderness, to the place where he was staying, at the mountain of God.
He sent word to Moses, saying, “Look, your father-in-law is coming to meet you, with your wife and your two sons with him.”
Moses went out to meet his father-in-law, bowed down to him, and kissed him. They greeted one another, and he brought them into the tent.

Moses told his father-in-law everything the Lord had done to Pharaoh and the Egyptians for Israel’s sake, all the hardship they had experienced on the journey, and how the Lord had rescued them from the power of Pharaoh and the Egyptians.
Jethro marveled at all the good things the Lord had done for them, because he had rescued them from the power of the Egyptians and from the power of Pharaoh, the king of Egypt.
Jethro said, “Blessed is the Lord, because he has rescued his people from the power of the Egyptians and from the power of Pharaoh.
Now I know that God is greater than all the gods, because he rose up against them.”
Then Jethro took burnt offerings and sacrifices to offer to God. Aaron and all the elders of Israel came to eat bread with Moses’ father-in-law in God’s presence.
And it happened on the following day that Moses sat down to judge the people, and all the people stood before Moses from morning until evening.
Jethro saw everything he was doing for the people and said to him, “What is this that you are doing for the people? Why do you sit while the people stand before you from morning until evening?”
Moses said to his father-in-law, “The people come to me to seek judgment from God.
For when they have a dispute, they come to me, and I judge each one and teach them God's commands and his law.”
Moses' father-in-law said to him, “You are not handling this matter properly.
You will wear yourself out completely and be unable to bear it—you and all these people who are with you. This task is too difficult for you, and you will not be able to do it alone.
So now listen to me, and I will give you advice, and may God be with you. Represent these people before God and bring their cases before God.
Explain God's commands and his law to them, and teach them the paths they are to walk in and the things they are to do.

Choose for yourself from among the people capable men who serve God, righteous men who hate pride. Appoint them over the people as leaders of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens, and let them judge the people at all times.
Let them bring the important matter to you, but let them judge the minor cases themselves. They will give you relief and share the burden with you.
If you do this, God will give you rest, and you will be able to stand firm, and all these people will go to their own place in peace.”
Moses listened to his father-in-law's advice and did what he had told him.
He chose capable men from all Israel and appointed them over the people as leaders of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens.
They judged the people at all times. They brought every important case before Moses, but they judged the smaller cases themselves.
Moses sent his father-in-law away, and he went to his own land.
In the third month after the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt, on that very day, they came to the wilderness of Sin.
They set out from Rephidim and came to the wilderness of Sinai. Israel camped there in front of the mountain.
Moses went up onto the mountain of God, and God called to him from the mountain, saying, “This is what you are to say to the house of Jacob and make known to the Israelites:
‘You have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I carried you as though on eagles' wings and gathered you to myself.
So now, if you truly obey my voice and keep my covenant, you will be my chosen people from among all the nations, for the whole earth is mine.
“You will be a kingdom and a priesthood for me, and a holy nation. These are the words you are to say to the Israelites.”
Moses came and called the elders of the people and set before them these words that God had commanded him.
All the people answered together, saying, “We will do everything God has said and obey it.” Moses reported all the people's words to God.
The Lord said to Moses, “Look, I am coming to you in a pillar of cloud, so that the people may hear me speaking with you and trust you forever.” Moses reported the people's words to the Lord.
The Lord said to Moses, “Go down and warn these people, and purify them today and tomorrow, and let them wash their clothes.”
Let them be ready for the third day, for on the third day the Lord will come down onto Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people.
You must set boundaries for all the people around it, saying, “Be careful not to go up the mountain or touch it, for anyone who touches it will surely die.”

No hand must touch him, for he must be stoned with stones or shot with arrows. Whether animal or human, he must not live. When the sounds and the trumpets and your cloud come, let them too go up the mountain.
Moses went down from the mountain to the people. He told them and purified them, and they washed their clothes.
He said to the people, “Be ready for three days. Do not approach your wives.”
On the morning of the third day, there were thunderclaps and flashes of lightning, and a dark cloud over Mount Sinai, and the sound of a trumpet.
Down, you and Aaron with you. But do not let the priests and the people dare to come up to God, lest the Lord destroy some of them.
Moses went down to the people and told them.
The Lord spoke all these words, saying:
“I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of your slavery.”
You must have no other gods besides me.
You must not make yourself an idol or a likeness of anything in heaven above, on the earth below, or in the water beneath the earth.

You must not bow down to them or serve them, for I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, who punishes the children for the sins of their fathers, down to the third and fourth generations of those who hate me,
and who shows mercy to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.
You must not use the name of the Lord your God for something worthless, for the Lord will not hold anyone guiltless who uses his name for something worthless.
Remember the Sabbath day and keep it holy.
For six days you must work and do all your work.

But the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God. You must not do any work on it—you, your son, your daughter, your male slave, your female slave, your ox, your donkey, any animal belonging to you, or the foreign resident living among you.
For in six days the Lord made heaven, earth, the sea, and everything in them, and he rested on the seventh day. Therefore the Lord blessed the seventh day and made it holy.
Honor your father and your mother, so that things may go well with you and you may live a long time on the good land that the Lord your God will give you.
You must not commit adultery.
You must not steal.
You must not murder.
You must not testify falsely against your neighbor with deceptive testimony.

You must not covet your neighbor’s wife. You must not covet your neighbor’s house, his field, his male slave, his female slave, his ox, his donkey, any animal belonging to him, or anything that belongs to your neighbor.
All the people saw the sound and the flashes, the sound of the trumpet, and the mountain giving off smoke. All the people were afraid and stood far away.
They said to Moses, “You speak with us, and do not let God speak with us, lest we die.”
Moses said to them, “Take courage, for God has come to you to test you, so that fear of him may be within you and you may not sin.”
All the people stood at a distance, but Moses went into the darkness, to the place where God was.
The Lord said to Moses, “This is what you are to say to the house of Jacob and make known to the Israelites: ‘You yourselves have seen that I spoke to you from heaven.’”
You must not make gods of silver or gods of gold for yourselves.

You are to make me an altar of earth and sacrifice on it your burnt offerings and your offerings for well-being, your sheep and your cattle. In every place where I proclaim my name, I will come to you and bless you.
If you make me an altar of stones, you must not build it with cut stones, because you have used a cutting tool on it, and it has become defiled.
You must not go up to my altar by steps, so that you do not expose your nakedness on it.’”
These are the regulations you are to set before them.
If you buy a Hebrew slave, he must serve you for six years. In the seventh year he must go free without payment.
If he comes in alone, he is also to go out alone. But if a wife comes in with him, his wife is also to go out with him.
If his master gives him a wife and she bears him sons or daughters, the wife and the children are to belong to her master, but he is to go out alone.
But if the slave answers and says, “I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out as a free man,”
his master is to bring him before God's tribunal. Then he is to bring him to the door that has a bolt, and his master is to pierce his ear with an awl. He is to serve him as a slave forever.
If someone sells his daughter as a slave, she must not go out as the male slaves do.
If she does not please her master, who agreed to take her for himself, he is to redeem her. He has no authority to sell her to a foreign nation, because he has broken faith with her.
If he agrees to give her to his son, he must treat her according to the ordinance concerning daughters.
If he takes another woman for himself, he must not reduce her provisions, her clothing, or his marital obligations to her.
If he does not do these three things for her, she is to go out freely, without paying any money.
If someone strikes another person and that person dies, he must be put to death in his place.
But if the one who did it was not acting under his own control, but God delivered the other person into his hands, then I will give you a place to which the person who kills may flee.
But if someone sets upon his neighbor to kill him by treachery and then flees to the altar, you are to take him away from my altar and put him to death.
Anyone who strikes his father or his mother must be put to death.
Anyone who curses his father or his mother must be put to death.
Whoever kidnaps one of the Israelites, takes him by force, and sells him, and is afterward found, must be put to death.
If two men curse one another and one strikes the other with a stone or with his fist, and the injured man does not die but takes to his bed,
if the man gets up and walks outside with a staff, the one who struck him is to be acquitted. However, he must pay for the man's lost time and medical treatment.
If someone strikes his male or female slave with a rod, and the slave dies under his hands, he must certainly be punished.
But if he remains alive for a day or two, they must not exact vengeance from his master, because he is his master's money.

If two men fight with one another and strike a pregnant woman, and her child comes out before it has taken shape, a penalty is to be imposed on him. He is to pay whatever the woman's husband demands of him, upon request.
But if it has taken form, he must give a life for a life.
An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, a hand for a hand, a foot for a foot.
A burn for a burn, a wound for a wound, a dark bruise for a dark bruise.
If someone strikes the eye of his male or female slave and blinds them, he must set them free in compensation for their eye.
If he knocks out the tooth of his male or female slave, he must set them free in compensation for their tooth.
If an ox gores a man or a woman and the person dies, the ox must be stoned to death, and its flesh must not be eaten. But the owner of the ox will be free of guilt.
But if the ox had been prone to goring before, and its owner had been warned but did not destroy it, and it kills a man or a woman, the ox must be stoned, and its owner must also be put to death.
But if a ransom is imposed on him, he must pay whatever ransom is imposed on him for his life.
If it gores a son or a daughter, he must be dealt with according to this law.
If the ox gores a male or female slave, he must give their owner fifteen silver staters, and the ox must be stoned.
If someone opens a pit, or digs a pit and does not cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls into it,
the owner of the pit must pay for them, or give money to their owner. The dead animal will belong to him.
If an ox gores another person's ox and it dies, he must sell the living ox, and they must divide its price between them. They must also divide the dead ox between them.
But if it was known that the ox had been prone to goring before, and its owner had been warned but did not destroy it, he must give an ox in place of the ox, and the dead animal will belong to him.
If someone steals an ox or a sheep and slaughters it or sells it, he must give five oxen for the ox and four sheep for the sheep.
If a thief is caught at the place where he has broken in, and he is struck and dies, this is not counted as murder against the person who struck him.
But if the sun has risen on him, the person who struck him is liable to death and must die in his place. But if the thief has nothing, he must be sold to pay for the theft.
If he is caught and the stolen animal is found in his possession, from a donkey down to a sheep, he must repay them alive, two for one.

If someone grazes livestock in a field or a vineyard and lets his animal eat in another field, he must make restitution from the field according to its produce. But if it eats the whole field, he must give the best of his field or the choicest produce of his vineyard.
If a fire breaks out and catches in thorns and burns threshing floors, standing grain, or a field, the person who lit the fire must replace what was burned.
If someone gives his neighbor money, gold, or utensils for safekeeping, and they are stolen from the man's house, then, if the person who took them is found, he must repay them double.
But if the person who took them is not found, the owner of the house must come before God and swear that he has not dealt dishonestly with any of his neighbor's property.

In every case of wrongdoing, whether concerning an ox, a donkey, a sheep, clothing, or any lost property over which a claim is made, the case of both parties must come before God. Whoever is convicted before God must repay his neighbor double.
If someone gives his neighbor a donkey, a calf, a sheep, or any animal to look after, and it dies or is carried off without anyone knowing,
